section_summary: This section documents U.S. efforts to monitor and restrict Japanese access to petroleum, strategic minerals, industrial fibers, and other supplies during mid-1941. It combines diplomatic and intelligence reporting on Japanese purchases in Latin America with correspondence about export controls, including negotiations to keep Colombian platinum from Japan in exchange for possible U.S. assistance obtaining silk or rayon. The section also records growing public and congressional pressure for a complete oil embargo and reports specific cargoes involving rock crystal, quicksilver, cobalt, ores, resin, and lubricating oil.

subfiles.title: Rio telegram clarifying reference to Japanese merchant vessels
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Washington; retransmitted to OPNAV
subfiles.about: Clarifies that an earlier report concerned Japanese merchant vessels rather than warships.
subfiles.summary: Caffery corrects the Department's understanding of his August 6 telegram, emphasizing that it referred to Japanese merchant vessels and not war vessels. Page 537 is the Navy retransmission or paraphrase of the same message.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese commercial activity in Brazil
subfiles.about: Reports Carlos Steinberg's information about Japanese stockpiling and mining interests in Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Steinberg states that Casa Tozan was exporting Brazilian goods to Lourenço Marques to build stocks nearer Japan and reduce blockade risks. He also reports that another Japanese concern controlled Brazilian mining interests, including mica at Carangola and a prospective nickel property in Goiás.

subfiles.title: Fitch telegram advocating a complete embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Mrs. George A. Fitch, New York
subfiles.about: Urges the State Department to impose a complete embargo on Japan even at the risk of war.
subfiles.summary: Fitch cites a recent Gallup poll, says the Department hasn't carried out the public's mandate for a complete embargo, and asks whether one can be expected.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply to Mrs. Fitch
subfiles.about: Explains that foreign-policy decisions cannot rest solely on public polling or the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Fitch's expression of confidence in Hull and himself. He stresses that foreign policy is made by the whole government after weighing law, authority, public opinion, capacity, practicability, and national welfare, and declines to promise a complete embargo.

subfiles.title: Bureau of the Budget letter concerning H.J. Res. 189
subfiles.from: Assistant Director, Legislative Reference, Bureau of the Budget
subfiles.about: Acknowledges State's views on legislation seeking to end petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Budget Bureau acknowledges Welles's July 3 response on H.J. Res. 189, urging the President to use export powers to stop petroleum shipments to Japan; a letter to the War Secretary is enclosed.

subfiles.title: British Embassy report on North Borneo hemp
subfiles.about: Reports the termination of hemp exports from Japanese estates in British North Borneo to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Thorold says British North Borneo hemp from Japanese estates was exportable until the crisis; Britain's Ministry of Supply will now buy all of it, ending shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Finletter acknowledgment of North Borneo hemp decision
subfiles.about: Thanks Thorold for confirming that North Borneo hemp shipments to Japan will stop.
subfiles.summary: Finletter acknowledges Thorold's August 7 letter, noting with appreciation that no more North Borneo hemp will go to Japan.

subfiles.title: British report on cobalt ore for Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports a large cobalt-ore consignment awaiting shipment from Santos to Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy confirms its Santos consul reports 105 tons of cobalt ore dispatched for Yokohama on a Japanese vessel, the largest Santos cobalt consignment yet.

subfiles.title: FBI report on rock crystal shipped to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a German-owned firm's shipment of Brazilian rock crystal to Japan.
subfiles.summary: FBI source: Emilio Schupp & Company shipped 198 cases of rock crystal, worth $23,520, on the Yamazuki Maru from Rio via Buenos Aires to M. Shinehara in Kofu on May 29.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Coordinator forwarding Margetts correspondence
subfiles.to: State Department, Division of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards correspondence urging that oil exports to Japan cease before rationing begins in the eastern United States.
subfiles.summary: Frey forwards Walter Margetts Jr.'s June 30 letter to Ickes to State, with a copy of the Petroleum Coordinator's reply.

subfiles.title: Margetts letter opposing rationing while Japan receives oil
subfiles.about: Requests that eastern oil rationing be deferred until oil and gasoline exports to Japan stop.
subfiles.summary: Margetts, for the Passaic Taxpayers and Renters Association, argues locals shouldn't bear rationing while Japan receives American petroleum, and asks Ickes to end those exports first.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Coordinator reply to Margetts
subfiles.from: John W. Frey, signed by Wright W. Gary
subfiles.about: Explains that the Atlantic Seaboard petroleum problem concerns tanker capacity rather than exports from California to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Petroleum Coordinator says Eastern shortages stem from tankers diverted to defense service, East Asia oil comes from California, export controls are State's, and no gasoline rationing is recommended.

subfiles.title: Treasury investigation of the Saer Hermanos platinum inquiry
subfiles.about: Reports Customs findings about a Colombian platinum transaction initially associated with Kanzo Ohno.
subfiles.summary: Treasury: a June 19 Saer Hermanos cable reached Scholtz & Company; Joseph Scholtz Jr. holds 443 ounces of Colombian platinum dust whose return-export license was rejected, and suggests German agents drive prices up and might route metal via Japan or Russia.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Bogotá enclosing Treasury's platinum report
subfiles.about: Transmits Treasury's confidential findings about Colombian platinum exports.
subfiles.summary: Airmail instruction to Bogota, citing the July 2 platinum despatch, encloses Gaston's August 19 confidential letter.

subfiles.title: Petroleum Coordinator forwarding Anderson letters
subfiles.about: Forwards George R. Anderson's letters about oil supplies to foreign countries.
subfiles.summary: Frey sends State two Anderson letters on foreign oil shipments referred by the Office of Production Management, with his notification to Anderson.

subfiles.title: Frey notification to George Anderson
subfiles.about: Tells Anderson that his letters have been forwarded to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Frey tells Anderson his June 4 and June 23 letters were forwarded to State, which has jurisdiction over foreign oil shipments.

subfiles.title: OPM referral of Anderson correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards Anderson's letters to the Petroleum Coordinator and requests a copy of the reply.
subfiles.summary: OPM's Nicol sends the Petroleum Coordinator Anderson's June 23 letter and June 4 letter to Roosevelt, asking acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Anderson letter to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Protests petroleum sales to Japan and also calls for legislation against defense-plant strikes.
subfiles.summary: Anderson cites clippings and the unlimited national emergency, says Americans shouldn't sacrifice while petroleum goes to Japan, and proposes compulsory measures against defense strikes.

subfiles.title: Anderson follow-up to Miss LeHand
subfiles.about: Requests a presidential answer to Anderson's earlier protest about Standard Oil sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Anderson tells Miss LeHand his June 4 letter to Roosevelt with Enquirer clippings on oil sales to Japan went unanswered and asks her to obtain a reply.

subfiles.title: State Department letter to OPM concerning Anderson
subfiles.to: Office of Production Management, attention Eric A. Nicol
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Anderson's letters and encloses the State Department's response.
subfiles.summary: State confirms receiving Anderson's June 4 and June 23 letters via the Petroleum Coordinator and returns copies of its reply.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Anderson
subfiles.about: Directs Anderson to the President's August 1 announcement on petroleum export regulations.
subfiles.summary: State acknowledges Anderson's two letters and encloses Roosevelt's August 1 announcement of new petroleum-export regulations.

subfiles.title: FBI report on rock crystal aboard Arabia Maru
subfiles.about: Reports a shipment of Brazilian rock crystal from Rio de Janeiro to Nagoya.
subfiles.summary: FBI source: Hachiya, Irmaos & Cia. shipped fifty-seven cases of rock crystal on the Arabia Maru from Rio about May 31 for a Nagoya firm.

subfiles.title: Referral of Samson Knoll's foreign-policy letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a Palo Alto correspondent's letter because it concerns U.S. foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: Frey forwards Samson Knoll's August 3 Palo Alto Teachers Union letter, with his reply advising Knoll of the referral.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of the Morris letter
subfiles.about: Submits W. F. Morris's communication for consideration and a report.
subfiles.summary: Senate referral of the Morris letter asks appropriate consideration and a report.

subfiles.title: Morris letter protesting oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why officials permit oil shipments to Japan and requests Connally's opinion.
subfiles.summary: Morris calls continued oil shipments to Japan appeasement and national cowardice and asks Connally's personal views.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Senator Connally
subfiles.about: Provides Roosevelt's August 1 petroleum-export announcement for use in answering W. F. Morris.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Connally's transmission of Morris's letter and encloses the President's August 1 petroleum-export announcement.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Bogotá on Colombian silk needs
subfiles.about: Requests an estimate of Colombia's short-term silk needs and proposes rayon as a possible substitute.
subfiles.summary: Telegram to Bogota: virtually no silk can be promised; asks Colombia's three-month need net of stocks, offers to seek rayon access, and stresses keeping platinum from other countries.

subfiles.title: Braden telegram on platinum-for-silk discussions
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for Thomas K. Finletter
subfiles.about: Reports President Santos's response to U.S. pressure against exchanging Colombian platinum for Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Braden told Santos no platinum could go to Japan; Santos warned lacking silk would close a mill and displace 284 workers, and the Foreign Minister said Japan would take only platinum for silk. Page 570 paraphrases it.

subfiles.title: FBI report on quicksilver shipped to Osaka
subfiles.about: Reports a June shipment of quicksilver from Mexico to Osaka.
subfiles.summary: FBI source: 673 flasks of quicksilver left a Mexican port, apparently Tampico, for Osaka on June 5; the rest of that month's exports went to the U.S.

subfiles.title: Lima despatch on Japanese orders for antimony and wolfram
subfiles.from: Julian Greenup for the U.S. Ambassador, Lima
subfiles.about: Provides banking details for Japanese-financed shipments of antimony and wolfram to Osaka.
subfiles.summary: Lima: Yokohama Specie Bank credits of $11,400 for 100 tons of antimony ore from Antofagasta to Osaka and $15,177 for ten tons of wolfram from Callao; enclosures reproduce the antimony instructions via a La Paz bank.

subfiles.title: Finletter letter forwarding the Lima minerals despatch
subfiles.about: Sends copies of the Lima Embassy's report on Japanese mineral orders in Bolivia and Peru.
subfiles.summary: Finletter encloses two copies of the August 18 Lima despatch on Japanese mineral orders in Bolivia and Peru.

subfiles.title: Lima report on resin being reshipped to Kobe
subfiles.from: Julian Greenup for the U.S. Ambassador, Lima
subfiles.about: Reports a New York-origin resin shipment routed through Callao for onward shipment to Kobe.
subfiles.summary: Lima: the Lobos discharged 178 drums of resin at Callao, from the Cefalu via Cristobal; British information says Mitsubishi Shoji's resin will be reshipped to Kobe on the Rakuyo Maru.

subfiles.title: Division of Controls routing note on Lima resin report
subfiles.from: A. E. Panpano, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Requests attention to the despatch's third paragraph and the information it requires.
subfiles.summary: Controls routing note draws attention to the third paragraph of the Lima report and asks that the information be supplied.

subfiles.title: Dobrin inquiry concerning petroleum exports and the Foreign Service
subfiles.about: Requests information about petroleum exports to Japan and the American Foreign Service.
subfiles.summary: Only the closing of Dobrin's letter is legible on page 577, while page 578 chiefly contains filing marks. The substance is recoverable from the Department's reply: Dobrin asked about petroleum exports to Japan and about the American Foreign Service.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Dobrin
subfiles.about: Answers Dobrin's petroleum-export question and redirects his request for trade statistics.
subfiles.summary: State sends Dobrin Roosevelt's August 1 petroleum-export announcement, refers him to Commerce for statistics, and promises a separate answer on his Foreign Service question.

subfiles.title: Braden telegram urging approval of a silk shipment
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, for Thomas K. Finletter
subfiles.about: Urges permission for a small silk shipment to Colombia after Colombia blocked platinum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Braden: Colombia's Foreign Minister says Santos is reluctant to intervene because his brother-in-law owns the mill; denying silk would be catastrophic and support charges of retroactive U.S. rules; Braden recommends granting it. Pages 582-583 paraphrase.

subfiles.title: American Republics memorandum on Colombia's platinum and silk problem
subfiles.from: J. C. Satterthwaite, Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: Recommends making a reasonable effort to supply Colombia with silk or rayon in return for keeping platinum from Japan.
subfiles.summary: American Republics memo: Colombia should get reasonable help obtaining silk or rayon, else it could trade platinum to Japan; U.S. rayon is a more durable solution. Page 585 asks for a workable political solution.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Latin American export-control cooperation
subfiles.about: Requests that Henry Chalmers be told how accurately a newspaper report describes U.S. export controls.
subfiles.summary: Henry Chalmers is preparing a memo arguing other American republics aren't doing enough to stop strategic exports to Japan; the writer asks Duggan how accurate a New York Times export-control account is.

subfiles.title: Representative Rich letter on oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks the Petroleum Coordinator whether large daily oil shipments to Japan will be curtailed.
subfiles.summary: Representative Rich recalls hearings on reported daily oil shipments to Japan and argues the U.S. may need the petroleum and Japan could use it against the country.

subfiles.title: Welles reply to Representative Rich
subfiles.about: Explains that all petroleum exports have required licenses since June 20.
subfiles.summary: Welles tells Rich petroleum exports are prohibited unless licensed, with decisions weighing supply, defense, consumption and foreign relations, and the problem is receiving careful attention.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of assistance on the special Axis-shipment report
subfiles.from: Office of the Administrator of Export Control
subfiles.about: Commends officials who worked after hours to prepare a special report on shipments to Axis powers.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum thanks Walter Simpson, Bernard Barton, Samuel Burk and Jack Darragh for supplying statistics, license data and newspaper searches for the Axis-shipment memorandum to General Maxwell.

subfiles.title: Hull letter to Senator Bone
subfiles.about: Returns Fidelia Frye's materials and encloses the Department's answer to her concerns about oil exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull refers to Bone's May 16 transmission of Fidelia Frye's letter on oil to Japan, enclosing the Department's direct reply and returning her materials.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Fidelia Frye
subfiles.from: Hallett Johnson for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Describes U.S. controls on exports of oil and munitions to Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Johnson tells Frye arms exports have needed licenses since 1935 and the 1940 act allows restricting defense materials; aviation fuel and lubricants are barred beyond the Western Hemisphere and British Empire, and other controls are adjusted.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Senator Maloney concerning Reverend Winchester
subfiles.about: Answers concerns about Japanese oil purchases and the availability of tankers for domestic needs.
subfiles.summary: Hull outlines licensing restrictions on aviation fuel, lubricating oil, and other petroleum products and says applications are evaluated for national-defense effects. He adds that Japan-bound cargoes cited by Winchester traveled in Japanese vessels that would not have been available for domestic oil transport. Winchester's letter is returned as an enclosure.

subfiles.title: London telegram on rubber supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Britain's refusal to press the Netherlands to increase rubber supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: London telegram: Britain's Tokyo ambassador is told to say Britain won't press the Dutch to raise East Indies rubber shipments, being concerned Japan helps Germany get rubber.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum comparing aid and exports to China, Japan, and Britain
subfiles.about: Uses Commerce statistics to contrast U.S. exports to China with much larger exports to Japan and Britain.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck: in 1938-1940 U.S. exports to Japan were about four times those to China, petroleum to Japan nearly equaling all exports to China, and China got about one unit of Lend-Lease for every 98-100 allocated elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Assistant Secretary's routing note
subfiles.about: Records that the Division of Controls saw no need to answer the preceding memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Evans notes Mr. Allen of Controls found nothing requiring an answer; the rest is routing and filing marks.

subfiles.title: Customs report on the Azuma Maru oil cargo
subfiles.from: C. M. Leinbach, Philadelphia Customs District
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Lists lubricating-oil cargo intended for Japan aboard the Azuma Maru and reports that loading was being held.
subfiles.summary: Customs declarations covered thousands of barrels of oil supplied by Sinclair and shipped by Standard-Vacuum Oil and Asano Bussan. Although the suppliers asserted that the lubricants were outside export-control regulations, Customs planned laboratory analysis. Treasury advised that the cargo would probably be detained and suggested deferring loading.

subfiles.title: Senator Guffey letter forwarding the Jobbins protest
subfiles.about: Forwards a Philadelphia manufacturer's protest against loading oil on the Azuma Maru.
subfiles.summary: Senator Guffey forwards Edward Jobbins's telegram from Wilson and Company and asks Ickes to give it appropriate consideration.

subfiles.title: Jobbins telegram protesting the Azuma Maru loading
subfiles.about: Protests exporting oil to Japan while a defense-industry factory faces fuel shortages.
subfiles.summary: Jobbins protests the Azuma Maru loading, saying his defense-producing company can't get fuel assurance for fall and winter and a shortage could close the plant.

subfiles.title: Welles reply to Senator Guffey
subfiles.about: Reports that the Azuma Maru was prevented from leaving Philadelphia with the disputed oil cargo.
subfiles.summary: Welles tells Guffey the Azuma Maru did not leave Philadelphia with the oil cargo and that since June 20 all petroleum exports need a license after defense review.

subfiles.title: Rosen letter demanding an end to oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Fred W. Rosen, Committee to Defend America
subfiles.about: Condemns continued petroleum exports to Japan as appeasement and a threat to China and U.S. security.
subfiles.summary: Rosen cites a sharp rise in gasoline shipments to Japan, calls oil the major exception to strategic export limits, and asks the government to reconcile it with Roosevelt's promise of aid to China.

subfiles.title: Finletter report to Clayton on Japanese mineral cargoes from Antofagasta
subfiles.about: Provides figures for strategic ores carried by Japanese vessels from Antofagasta.
subfiles.summary: Finletter lists February 1941 Antofagasta cargoes of antimony, copper, lead and wolfram on Japanese ships, totaling several thousand long tons; the antimony came from Bolivia.

subfiles.title: Watson, Geach letter and tables on Chilean and Peruvian ore shipments
subfiles.about: Supplies statistics on Chilean and Peruvian ores and concentrates shipped to Japan from January 1940 through April 1941.
subfiles.summary: The Chilean table lists antimony, copper bars, copper concentrates and ores, molybdenum, manganese, and mercury, distinguishing Mauricio Hochschild's tonnage from other shippers. The Peruvian table similarly covers antimony, wolfram, lead-silver, copper concentrates and ores, molybdenum, and vanadium. The figures were sent in response to Mauricio Hochschild's June 5 letter.

subfiles.title: Copy of Watson, Geach ore-shipment letter and tables
subfiles.about: Duplicates the letter and statistical tables on Chilean and Peruvian mineral shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the cover letter referring to Mauricio Hochschild's June 5 communication. Its tables reproduce the January 1940-April 1941 totals for Chilean and Peruvian antimony, copper, wolfram, lead-silver, molybdenum, manganese, mercury, and vanadium shipments.

subfiles.title: Mauricio Hochschild letter on Japanese purchases of South American ores
subfiles.about: Explains the commercial conditions that enabled Japan to dominate purchases of Chilean and Bolivian ores.
subfiles.summary: Mauricio Hochschild says Japanese buyers took nearly all Chilean copper ores since 1936 by outbidding U.S. smelters, describes efforts to redirect trade to the U.S. and new manganese buying, and begins on Bolivian antimony; it continues past page 615.
